articles.title: Microsoft releases new Nvidia-chip AI PCs with revamped Windows 11 - TechCrunch
articles.summary: Microsoft releases new Nvidia-chip AI PCs with revamped Windows 11  TechCrunchThe tech industry wants you to run AI models at home, but it’s not for everyone  Yahoo FinanceNVIDIA, Microsoft Kick Off a New Beginning for Windows PCs With RTX Spark and AI Agents  NVIDIA BlogBuilding Windows for hybrid intelligence  Windows BlogMicrosoft to sell $2,599 Surface Laptop Ultra containing Nvidia AI chip  CNBC
articles.full_text:
Back in June, Nvidia announced that it had secured agreements with Microsoft and a host of other PC makers to develop AI- and agent-ready PCs for Windows based on its RTX Spark chip, but details on the machines were scant at the time.
On Wednesday, at an event held in San Francisco during the city’s Tech Week, Microsoft revealed the specs and price for its new Surface Laptop Ultra. The PC comes in two base models, one that starts at $2,600 and one with a more powerful chip that starts at $3,700. Prices rise from there with options for more memory and storage, up to $5,900. (Microsoft says the highest-end device is already out of stock.)
Microsoft also revealed its new workstation powered by the RTX Spark chip: the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, which starts priced at $6,000 and comes equipped with Microsoft dev tools like VS Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, WSL, and PowerShell 7.
The pitch for both this PC and workstation is that they are designed to run AI models on-device locally (and for free) with the CPU, GPU, unified memory, and other hardware modifications, like superior cooling, necessary to handle them.
Plus, they are running a revamped version of Windows 11 that includes a feature called “Execution Containers.” This makes it easier to sandbox AI agents, the company says. That feature will be available for all Windows 11 users, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at the event.
Nadella explained: “One of the things we realized in the last 3-4 years is that just having a model doesn’t do much for anything. You really do need to orchestrate, and you need to have memory outside of the model. You need to have this harnessed layer that is able to take multiple models plus context, plus memory, and the action space.”
He added that Microsoft is enabling that “not just for our apps but apps for anyone’s agent. That’s what the Windows platform is all about going forward.”
The devices are clearly aimed at developers, so much so that Microsoft is offering up to $1,000 off to people who trade in a MacBook Pro, as Macs have become a popular choice for developers and AI agent enthusiasts, particularly in Silicon Valley.
Still, these Surface PCs, with such powerful graphics processing, are also capable of content creation, video processing, and gaming, the company promises.
Microsoft wasn’t the only PC company to announce the specs for its new Nvidia-RTX Spark AI Windows PCs on Wednesday. Dell also announced the details of its previously announced Dell XPS 16 Creator Edition PC. It’s available for preorder now for a later October delivery at Best Buy, priced at $3,800.

articles.title: Why is artificial intelligence failing to transform enterprise productivity? - BCS, The Chartered Institute for IT
articles.summary: Why is artificial intelligence failing to transform enterprise productivity?  BCS, The Chartered Institute for IT

source_detail.name: BCS, The Chartered Institute for IT

articles.full_text:
If AI can draft reports, write code and automate routine tasks, why aren't organisations becoming dramatically more productive? The answer lies in leadership, culture and skills.
Summary
- While AI helps individuals automate tasks, organisations see significant productivity improvements only when they redesign workflows, operating models, and service delivery around new capabilities
- The AI productivity paradox reflects a recurring pattern in technology adoption
- Like email, office automation, and earlier computing innovations, AI often shifts work rather than eliminates it, while organisational adaptation struggles to match the pace of technological advancemen
- Effective AI adoption depends on governance, measurement, and cultural readiness
Despite the hype around generative artificial intelligence, organisations are noticing that overall productivity figures remain stubbornly flat. 
Recent survey data from BCS, the Chartered Institute for IT, covering over 600 IT professionals, reveals that productivity gains from artificial intelligence remain modest. These gains occur mainly at the individual level through personal task automation, draft summarisation, and code generation, rather than across the enterprise.
This gap between technical capability and business output is not a new phenomenon.
In the podcast Insight Exchange by BCS, host Martin Cooper MBCS speaks with James Freed FBCS, deputy director at the NHS Digital Academy within NHS England. They discuss this productivity paradox.
Along the way, James points out that adopting digital interventions involves both risk and opportunity. Many leadership teams view artificial intelligence as a simple tool to reduce wage costs, yet those savings never materialise if the underlying operational model stays identical.
Technology alone does not generate efficiency. Deploying sophisticated tools into legacy workflows accelerates the pace of outdated processes. A traditional example is bank operations: financial institutions achieved true productivity gains only when they shifted entirely to online banking and systematically closed physical branches, fundamentally altering how services were delivered to consumers.
Is the AI productivity paradox a modern phenomenon?
The discrepancy between technological investment and measurable output mirrors historical patterns across computing history.
Nobel laureate economist Robert Solow famously remarked in 1987 that the computer age could be seen everywhere except in the productivity statistics.
Archives from BCS demonstrate that similar concerns surfaced during the introduction of early silicon chips, visual display units, and automated office equipment throughout the 1970s and 1980s.
A key factor driving this paradox is the hidden administrative overhead that accompanies new tools. Early office computing innovations, such as the introduction of email, were expected to save vast amounts of time. Instead, while email revolutionised communication, it created new work patterns. Employees began spending hours daily reading, typing, and managing message inboxes, shifting human effort rather than eliminating it.
It’s also worth noting, James explained, that technology advances at an exponential pace. Gordon Moore identified this trajectory in the late 1960s, noting that chip component density doubles roughly every two years. By contrast, human capacity to adapt and absorb change grows at a much slower rate. As the gap between technological potential and organisational absorption widens, businesses struggle to keep pace, attempting to evaluate hundreds of new tools without the capacity to embed them successfully.
What structural barriers stop organisations from realising AI gains?
Research across multiple industries indicates that approximately 70 per cent of digital transformation initiatives fail to achieve their objectives. Around a quarter fail to realise even half of their target benefits. Crucially, roughly three-fifths of these failures stem directly from cultural and skills deficits rather than technical flaws or budget shortages.
To overcome these barriers, enterprise architect teams and senior leaders must address three core operational gaps:
- Digital skills deficits: over 20 million working adults in the UK lack the basic digital skills required for modern employment. Organisations cannot expect advanced AI adoption when baseline digital literacy remains uneven across the workforce. Collaborative initiatives with organisations like FutureDotNow focus on closing these essential skill gaps.
- Unaligned leadership strategy: senior leaders must select specific technologies that address defined operational challenges rather than pursuing generic digital adoption. Strategy must dictate technology choices, not the other way around.
- Lack of professional standards: Digital, data, and technology roles require formal professionalisation to ensure consistent capabilities across teams. Within NHS England, over 35,000 digital and data staff historically worked under thousands of different job titles, creating confusion and inconsistent standards.
How can senior leaders manage AI adoption effectively?
Leadership teams often feel uncomfortable navigating rapid digital change because many executives lack formal technology backgrounds. However, managing digital change requires applying rigorous governance rather than mastering code.
Leaders, the podcast found, must treat digital initiatives as strategic investments carrying inherent risks that require balanced portfolio management.
                                            For you
Be part of something bigger, join BCS, The Chartered Institute for IT.
James said: ‘And what we do with a lot of digital projects is we don't bother counting our winnings. We don't know whether we've won or not a lot of the time... If you don't measure the benefit, Solow's productivity paradox will come true.’
Effective management requires tracking concrete metrics rather than assuming benefits will naturally occur. Organisations routinely spend substantial capital on software deployments without establishing baseline measurements or post-implementation reviews. Without tracking specific outcomes, leadership teams cannot ascertain whether investments produced meaningful returns or merely increased operational complexity.
Furthermore, leadership must conduct rigorous user research before making procurement decisions. Investing in thorough discovery phases prevents organisations from spending resources on tools that do not solve genuine end-user problems.
Why are professional standards essential for safe AI implementation?
In highly regulated sectors like health and social care, poor technology implementation carries severe consequences. Operational errors in clinical settings can jeopardise patient safety.
Consequently, establishing professional standards across digital, data, and technology roles is critical for public safety and operational reliability.
To establish accountability, NHS England sets expectations that digital professionals hold professional body memberships, such as with BCS, and register with overarching bodies like the Federation for Informatics Professions (FEDIP). Standardising role titles, capability frameworks, and accreditation paths allows organisations to deploy talent efficiently and maintain clear operating guidelines.
Professionalisation ensures that multidisciplinary teams remain outcome focused, working within ethical guidelines and established safety protocols when deploying artificial intelligence.
How do organisations build a culture ready for digital change?
Technology cannot fix an organisational culture that is unready for change. Culture represents the everyday habits and behaviours within a business. To benefit from technology, organisations must build an environment defined by data-led decision making, curiosity, and humility.
Curious and humble organisations constantly evaluate their processes by asking clear, direct questions:
- Why are we performing this task in this specific way?
- What evidence supports our current operating model?
- Can we prove that our recent changes improved performance compared to yesterday?
- Are we open to adopting better methods suggested by frontline staff?
When teams are encouraged to challenge existing processes and test hypotheses using real data, they create the necessary conditions for successful digital adoption. Technology becomes an enabler of streamlined workflows rather than a layer of added frustration.
Ultimately, achieving productivity gains from artificial intelligence relies on human factors rather than software features. Tools provide opportunity, but people, leadership, process redesign, and cultural readiness determine whether that potential translates into measurable business performance.

articles.title: SpaceX is calling out other satellite operators for nearly crashing into Starlink - Business Insider
articles.summary: SpaceX is calling out other satellite operators for nearly crashing into Starlink  Business Insider
articles.full_text:
SpaceX is calling out rival satellite launchers after a series of near-miss collisions with its Starlink network.
In a blog post published on Tuesday, Elon Musk's rocket company warned that operators who don't share their satellites' trajectories are playing a dangerous game of chicken in Earth's orbit.
SpaceX, which has around 11,000 Starlink satellites in orbit, said that the satellite internet network has had potential near-miss collisions with about 650 satellites this year, half of which did not share their position.
In its blog post, SpaceX flagged two particularly dangerous near-misses.
In August, one of its satellites came within 134 meters of another satellite, with the Starlink satellite forced to rotate its arrays to a "knife-edge profile" to duck out of the way of its neighbor after it unexpectedly changed direction.
SpaceX said a Starlink satellite narrowly missed another object in October 2025, after the other satellite changed its trajectory to put it on a path that would have passed within 57 meters of the Starlink relay.
However, we cannot mitigate risk when another operator maneuvers without sharing a predicted trajectory that includes the burn.
This is the biggest risk in LEO pic.twitter.com/5sqbmW1aD7
— Starlink (@Starlink) October 6, 2026
SpaceX makes data on the trajectories of its Starlink satellites publicly available, but not every operator does, and the company said these gaps are increasing the risk of a catastrophic collision.
Astronomers have for years warned that the growing number of objects in orbit increases the risk of a runaway cascade of satellite collisions, creating a cloud of debris that could make some parts of Earth's orbit unusable or even block humanity's access to space entirely.
In its blog post, SpaceX said that its Starlink network had observed around 164,000 potential near-miss collisions over the past six months. The company said that it had reached out to other operators to alert them of flaws in their collision screening, some of which they were not aware of until SpaceX informed them.
It's not the first time SpaceX has railed against a lack of space in space. The Starship launcher said in January it would move around 4,400 Starlink satellites to reduce the risk of collisions, months after a near-miss with nine Chinese satellites.
According to data published by SpaceX, the vast majority of satellites that had close encounters with Starlink this year, which did not share their trajectory data, originated in China.
SpaceX has also faced complaints in the past about the orbits of its Starlink satellites. In 2021, China complained to the United Nations that two Starlink satellites had nearly collided with the country's Tiangong space station.
SpaceX is gearing up to massively expand Starlink, which is already the world's largest satellite constellation by far. Elon Musk has said the rocket giant plans to launch up to 100,000 Starlink satellites and as many as one million orbital data centers in the coming years.

articles.summary: SpaceX calls for better coordination in orbit after near-misses with Starlink  Ars TechnicaStarlink's plan to avoid orbital near-misses: Ephemeris sharing  The RegisterSpaceX is calling out other satellite operators for nearly crashing into Starlink  Business InsiderSpaceX warns of collision risk as satellites begin to crowd Earth's orbit  WESHSpaceX Identifies Unshared Ephemeris Data as Primary Orbital Collision Hazard in Low Earth Orbit  SatNew...
articles.full_text:
Space has plenty of room for more megaconstellations, but only if all operators are willing to share information about where their satellites are and where they’re going, a top executive at SpaceX and its AI subsidiary said this week.
Michael Nicolls, SpaceX’s vice president for Starlink and president of Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company, xAI, used a presentation Tuesday at the International Astronautical Congress in Turkey as a clarion call for improved data-sharing among satellite operators.
SpaceX’s Starlink constellation now has more than 11,000 satellites, about two-thirds of all active spacecraft in low-Earth orbit. Radars and telescopes routinely track thousands more pieces of space junk.
Starlink is, by far, the largest satellite constellation in operation today. But if you buy the buzz, Starlink is just the tip of the iceberg. SpaceX has revealed plans to launch up to a million satellites for a new constellation, called Starmind, to deploy AI computing capacity in low-Earth orbit. Amazon is in the early stages of launching a network of thousands of satellites to compete with Starlink, and two Chinese megaconstellations are now in full-scale deployment.
Law of large numbers
All of this raises the question of how to mitigate the risk of a collision in orbit, an event that could create thousands more pieces of space junk, potentially triggering a self-perpetuating cycle of debris generation. The risk of a collision on any given day is fantastically low. Space is vast and empty, and low-Earth orbit is a long way from filling up. SpaceX and most other Western operators de-orbit their rockets and satellites at the end of their missions to prevent additional debris in orbit.
“That said, the law of large numbers says that if it can happen, it will happen,” Nicolls said.
There’s still a long way to go to improve tracking, awareness, and coordination in orbit. This is sometimes called space traffic management. No global treaties or regulations require satellites to broadcast their locations and maneuvers or mandate coordination among satellite operators. Without rules of the road, it is up to governments and companies to set norms of behavior.

articles.title: Department of War dishes out $1.5 billion loan commitment to boost semiconductor supply chain — Wolfspeed to focus on national security applications as part of 30-year agreement - Tom's Hardware
articles.summary: Department of War dishes out $1.5 billion loan commitment to boost semiconductor supply chain — Wolfspeed to focus on national security applications as part of 30-year agreement  Tom's Hardware
articles.full_text:
U.S. Semiconductor Manufacturer Wolfspeed Inc. has received a conditional 30-year, $1.5 billion loan commitment letter from the U.S. Department of War (DoW) through its Office of Strategic Capital (OSC), as the country continues its push to boost domestic semiconductor manufacturing. According to an official press release on Oct. 7, Wolfspeed — which specializes in silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN) materials and devices — will use the long term-financing to upgrade its GaN epitaxy capabilities and to develop radiation hardening capabilities for current SiC and future GaN products.
The company says SiC and related technologies are “critical to next generation power and radio-frequency applications across defense, aerospace, AI, critical infrastructure and other strategic commercial markets,” and that it will focus on U.S. national security applications, including communications infrastructure and electronic warfare systems. “SiC and GaN have critical national security applications,” said Wolfspeed CEO Robert Feurle. “With this financing, the company would be well positioned to not only continue to serve the DoW but also expand its capabilities for the benefit of U.S. national security as a whole,” he continued.
Under the terms of the loan — which is subject to final agreements — Wolfspeed is required to issue the DoW warrants to buy up to 7.5% of its fully diluted equity. The warrants would be priced off the stock's volume-weighted average price (VWAP) and handed over in proportion to each tranche of the loan as it's funded. As of this report, the loan remains conditional, pending the OSC’s completion of its due diligence. Wolfspeed also needs to secure government approvals and appropriations, as well as the consent of its existing lenders. The company itself warns there's no guarantee the financing will go through.
“This conditional 30-year commitment represents another significant milestone in our ongoing efforts to optimize Wolfspeed’s capital structure and improve our financial foundation,” said Wolfspeed CFO Gregor van Issum. “Subject to the satisfaction of diligence, negotiation of definitive agreements, and other financial, legal, and investment conditions, the broader commitment is expected to provide additional long-dated capital to support our strategic priorities, improve financial flexibility, and further position Wolfspeed for long-term value creation.”
The announcement marks the U.S.’s latest move to onshore critical semiconductor manufacturing and strengthen the domestic supply chain, combining direct capital subsidies, major tax incentives, and strict regulatory changes. Through the $54.2 billion CHIPS and Science Act, the U.S. government has injected billions into massive fabrication facilities for industry leaders like TSMC, Intel, GlobalFoundries, and Micron, while simultaneously utilizing the Section 48D Advanced Manufacturing Investment Credit to offer a 25% tax credit that has led to over $827 billion in private sector announcements.

articles.title: With ASTRALINK, Turkey prepares its own military “Starlink” with 198 satellites - Meta-Defense
articles.summary: With ASTRALINK, Turkey prepares its own military “Starlink” with 198 satellites  Meta-Defense
articles.full_text:
The use of Starlink by Ukrainian forces has demonstrated the operational usefulness of a network comprising numerous satellites in low Earth orbit, particularly for maintaining communications where ground infrastructure is unavailable. Despite the electronic warfare capabilities now deployed by Russia to disrupt these links, this American model operated by SpaceX is inspiring programs in China, Turkey, India and Germany. These initiatives now combine secure military communications, sovereign infrastructure and industrial capabilities able to produce and then replenish several hundred satellites.
Table of contents
ASELSAN’s ASTRALINK: first launch in two years
In Turkey, defense electronics group ASELSAN is developing ASTRALINK, a satellite system intended for military users located beyond the direct reach of ground networks. The satellites are to connect these users to network centers with secure, uninterrupted, low-latency and high-capacity communications. The program is being conducted as part of work on low Earth orbit satellites and 5G and 6G military communications, with the objective of creating a national solution distinct from American Starlink.
Speaking at the International Astronautical Congress held in Antalya on October 6, 2026, ASELSAN President and CEO Ahmet Akyol linked this expansion to the group’s historic activities. “Our experience as a defense electronics company has provided us with a solid foundation for developing technologies for the space domain,” he said. The Turkish company also intends to use these capabilities to seek new international opportunities beyond the needs expressed by its country’s armed forces and government agencies.
The announced constellation is to comprise 198 satellites to ensure resilient communications over Turkish territory and partner countries. Ahmet Akyol outlined its timeline during his address in Antalya. “We began implementing this project at the end of last year. Our constellation will comprise 198 satellites in low Earth orbit. The first launch is planned within two years,” he said. ASELSAN is also targeting scalable industrial capacity capable of producing up to 4 satellites each month.
National programs versus the Starlink model
Turkish engineers must develop the waveform, chips, software algorithms, antenna receivers and other subsystems required for ASTRALINK. ASELSAN states that it already controls a chain ranging from space-qualified electronic components to platforms, payloads and ground infrastructure. The group also supplies the imaging radar, secure transmission equipment and the main security unit for the GÖKTÜRK-3 satellite, while contributing to the TÜRKSAT-6A and TÜRKSAT-7A geostationary communications satellites.
China, for its part, is continuing the deployment of the GuoWang constellation, operated by the state-owned China Satellite Network Group. On September 17, 2026, a Long March 12 launcher reportedly placed nine new satellites into low Earth orbit from the Wenchang commercial launch site, bringing the number of deployed spacecraft to 204, either operational or still ascending to their final orbit. Intended to provide Internet services worldwide, GuoWang is initially intended to cover the Chinese market and relies on several categories of satellite platforms.
In Germany, OHB and Rheinmetall created the OHB Rheinmetall Space Networks GmbH joint venture in Bremen in spring 2026 to address the Bundeswehr’s military communications needs. It is to handle the architecture, development, integration, delivery and operation of the future SATCOMBw Level 4 system, including its cybersecurity. A bid has been submitted to the Federal Ministry of Defence, while German projects could reach up to 1,200 communications and intelligence satellites, with more than €35 billion in space investments by 2030.
France is instead moving towards a hybrid architecture combining Syracuse military satellites, placed in geostationary orbit, and Eutelsat’s OneWeb constellation in low Earth orbit. Launched in June 2025, the Nexus project led on June 15, 2026 to the signing of the Centaure contract between the Direction générale de l’armement and the European operator. This 8-year contract, capped at €350 million and including an initial firm commitment of €138 million over 4 years, grants the French armed forces exclusive and priority access to part of OneWeb’s resources.
Europe and Russia accelerate sovereign constellations
The draft update to France’s 2024-2030 Military Programming Law also provides €3.9 billion for space capabilities, an increase of around 50%. Part of this effort is intended to secure OneWeb for the communications required for collaborative combat and intelligence. At the European level, an additional €1 billion is to support the constellation over the next decade. Eutelsat has also ordered 229 satellites from Airbus Defence and Space, bringing to 669 the number of new OneWeb spacecraft entrusted to the European manufacturer since 2024.
This capability must remain available during the development of the European IRIS² constellation, which is expected to enter service in mid-2032. Airbus, Leonardo and Thales are also preparing their space-sector rapprochement under the Bromo project, publicly supported by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in September 2026. The three groups are seeking to form an industrial entity better able to compete with SpaceX, while satellite orders, ground infrastructure and secure services remain divided among several European players.
Finally, Russia is developing Rassvet, a low Earth orbit network designed by Bureau 1440 and presented as a national equivalent of Starlink. Ukrainian sources reported in August 2026 that 12 satellites had reached their operational altitude and 3 others were still ascending. Moscow plans to expand this constellation to 250 spacecraft in 2027, 730 in 2030 and more than 900 in 2035, while strengthening its ground-based electronic warfare capabilities intended to disrupt the satellite communications used by Ukrainian forces.
ASTRALINK is thus part of a set of national programs adopting the distributed architecture proven by Starlink, without necessarily replicating its commercial model. ASELSAN must still launch its first satellites and then progressively deploy the 198 announced spacecraft before achieving full coverage. Its planned capacity of 4 units per month, combined with components and infrastructure developed in Turkey, should enable the group to meet national needs while offering its system to partner countries and international markets.

articles.title: Most Americans think artificial intelligence is developing too fast, a new AP-NORC poll finds - Bozeman Daily Chronicle
articles.summary: Most Americans think artificial intelligence is developing too fast, a new AP-NORC poll finds  Bozeman Daily Chronicle
articles.full_text:
Most Americans think artificial intelligence is developing too fast, a new AP-NORC poll finds
A new AP-NORC poll finds that most Americans think artificial intelligence is developing too fast
A new AP-NORC poll finds that most Americans think artificial intelligence is developing too fast. And the vast majority of U.S. adults say it's highly important for the government to ensure that AI stays under human control and that U.S. workers are protected. Despite bipartisan concern about the speed of AI's development, few Americans think either major political party is better equipped to handle artificial intelligence. President Donald Trump also has a low approval rating on the issue, as even leaders of the companies that are developing frontier AI models are calling for a slowdown so government regulation can catch up.
WASHINGTON (AP) — Worries around artificial intelligence cross party lines, with the vast majority of Americans saying the U.S. government should prioritize keeping AI under human control and protecting workers.
A new poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research finds that most Americans, 64%, think AI is developing “too fast,” while 27% say its development has been “about right” and only 8% say it's moving “too slow.”
The risk that powerful AI models could evade human control and hurt humanity, once the stuff of science fiction, has been emerging as a more pressing concern. Even leaders of the companies that are developing frontier AI models are calling for a slowdown so that government regulation can catch up. President Donald Trump has pushed back against slowing down AI development because of concerns that China will gain an advantage with the technology. Data centers powering AI projects have also taken a prominent role in major political races as the midterm elections approach.
About 8 in 10 U.S. adults say it's “extremely” or “very” important for the U.S. government to ensure that AI stays under human control, and they are about as likely to want the government to prioritize protecting the country's workforce. Most U.S. adults also think minimizing environmental harm and growing the U.S. economy are highly important. About half say this about promoting technological innovation, and slightly fewer say that about competing with China.
There's bipartisan concern about the speed of AI's development, but few Americans think either major political party has an advantage in handling artificial intelligence. Trump, a Republican, also gets a low rating on his handling of the issue, with 67% of U.S. adults disapproving of his performance on AI.
Stephanie Stewart, a junior-high science teacher in Sunset, Utah, said she is frustrated by the president’s opposition to AI regulation.
“There is no handling of the issue except for we’re just going to allow these companies to do whatever they want, and we’re not going to regulate them,” said Stewart, 53.
Most say protecting workers should be a priority for the government
Ron Theusch, a truck driver who lives in rural Alden, Minnesota, said his No. 1 concern with AI is the potential loss of jobs — including his own.
“I can just see a train of self-driving trucks 24/7, just running up and down I-35, loading and unloading. I can just see that happening,” said Theusch, 58.
Most Democrats and Republicans agree on the importance of protecting workers and keeping AI under human control, the poll found.
“There was a movie called ‘Terminator,’ where the robots came back and killed everybody,” Theusch said. “People relate to that ... I don’t know where it’s going to land. I really don’t have anything I can do to control it, you know. It’s going to evolve.”
There's less consensus about the importance of other priorities when it comes to AI. Republicans are more likely than Democrats to say it’s highly important to grow the U.S. economy and to compete with other countries like China. Democrats, on the other hand, are more likely to say it’s at least “very” important to minimize environmental harm.
“I don’t understand how, because they’re doing something as well as us, that we can’t be more human about it and more humane about it than just to say, ‘Well, they’re doing it, so we have to do it,’” Stewart said of U.S. competition with China.
And while about three-quarters of Democrats say AI is developing “too fast,” only about half of Republicans share that worry. People under 30 years old also express higher levels of concern than people 60 or older, the survey found.
“I think I have all the normal concerns, right? I think it’s wonderful for certain applications, but I also feel like it will be overused and can create a lack of personal connections. It can make people lazy because information is just given to them without really having to research things on their own,” said Kelly Opp, a 62-year-old Republican in Albuquerque, New Mexico.
“Like everything else, once you get that ball rolling, it progresses fast on its own, but I think that it will continue to keep progressing. So the speed doesn’t really bother me,” she said.
Americans have little confidence in Democrats or Republicans on AI
As a teacher, Stewart regularly uses AI to help with her work, including with creating assignments or assisting with tests. But she is deeply concerned about AI's effects on children.
“You’ve got to protect kids. You’ve got to protect teens. You've got to protect privacy ... we need to try to do something,” she said.
Americans have little trust in either party when it comes to the handling of AI issues. About 4 in 10 Americans say they don’t trust either the Democratic Party or the Republican Party on AI, according to the poll, while nearly 2 in 10 trust both parties equally, and the rest are split between trusting the Republicans and the Democrats.
Even people who identify with the parties are ambivalent about their ability to handle the issue. Only about half of Republicans and Democrats say their party is better equipped to handle AI issues, and roughly 3 in 10 in each case say neither party is.
“I am kind of moderate. And I see that there’s good on both sides," said Stewart. "Anyone back in Washington is weak on doing anything for anyone but themselves right now. So, no, I don’t think the Democrats would do a better job per se. Maybe they would definitely tout it. But until I see anything coming from anyone, I’m going to be like, ‘Yeah, no. You’re all just sitting there.’”

articles.title: Thin-Film Chemicals Market To 2035: Advanced Node Semiconductor Scaling Drives Growth - News and Statistics - IndexBox
articles.summary: Thin-Film Chemicals Market To 2035: Advanced Node Semiconductor Scaling Drives Growth - News and Statistics  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
Abstract
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Thin-Film Chemicals market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global thin-film chemicals market is undergoing a structural transformation, driven by the semiconductor industry's relentless pursuit of advanced node scaling and the proliferation of thin-film deposition technologies across electronics, optics, and energy applications. Thin-film chemicals, defined as high-purity chemical precursors and materials used in deposition processes such as chemical vapor deposition (CVD) and atomic layer deposition (ALD), are critical enablers of transistor gate dielectrics, interconnect barriers, and advanced packaging layers.
Demand is no longer a simple function of wafer starts but is increasingly tied to the number of deposition steps per node and the performance specifications of next-generation devices. OEM demand is bifurcating into two distinct streams: high-volume, cost-optimized applications for mature nodes and low-volume, high-performance, validation-intensive applications for sub-5nm logic, 3D NAND, and advanced memory. Each stream carries vastly different qualification burdens, pricing models, and supply chain expectations. Supply chain resilience has emerged as a primary strategic concern, superseding pure cost optimization.
The validation-sensitive nature of electronic-grade thin-film chemicals creates severe bottlenecks; a disruption in a single specialty precursor can halt production for entire fab lines, leading chipmakers and OEMs to actively pursue dual-sourcing and regional localization strategies. The aftermarket and retrofit channel represents a fragmented but high-margin growth vector, particularly for performance and durability-enhancing coatings in legacy fabs and specialty devices.
However, route-to-market is complex, relying on a network of specialist distributors, applicators, and certification bodies, with economics heavily dependent on service bundling and brand reputation rather than raw material cost. Competitive advantage is shifting from broad chemical supply to integrated solution provision. Winners are those who can co-develop materials with fab process engineers, navigate the multi-year validation gauntlet, and provide robust technical support and traceability throughout the product lifecycle. Pure-play chemical suppliers face margin compression and disintermediation. Geographic production and consumption patterns are decoupling.
While final device assembly may be concentrated in specific regions, the manufacturing and R&D for the underlying thin-film components—and thus the chemical inputs—are clustering in established electronics and semiconductor hubs, creating critical pinch points in the global supply web. Regulatory and standards compliance is evolving from a baseline quality hurdle to a core performance differentiator. Standards governing purity, particle contamination, and environmental health and safety are becoming more stringent, favoring suppliers with advanced purification capabilities and robust quality management systems.
The baseline scenario for the global thin-film chemicals market anticipates robust growth over the forecast period 2026-2035, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 6.8%, culminating in a market index of 193.2 by 2035 (2025=100). This outlook is underpinned by the semiconductor industry's capital expenditure cycle, which is expected to remain elevated as foundries and IDMs ramp advanced nodes (3nm, 2nm, and beyond) and expand capacity for memory (3D NAND, DRAM) and advanced packaging. Each technology node transition typically increases the number of deposition steps and the complexity of precursor chemistries, driving volume and value growth.
Additionally, the proliferation of thin-film applications in adjacent markets—such as display technologies (OLED, microLED), photovoltaics (perovskite, CIGS), and optical coatings—provides a diversified demand base that mitigates cyclicality in any single end market. Regionally, Asia-Pacific will continue to dominate both production and consumption, accounting for over 60% of global demand, driven by the concentration of semiconductor fabrication in Taiwan, South Korea, China, and Japan.
North America and Europe will see moderate growth, supported by government initiatives to onshore semiconductor manufacturing (e.g., US CHIPS Act, EU Chips Act) and the presence of leading specialty chemical suppliers. Latin America and the Middle East & Africa will remain niche markets, with growth opportunities in electronics assembly and specialty coatings. The baseline scenario assumes no major global recessions, continued technology investment, and a stable regulatory environment. However, risks such as trade tensions, raw material supply disruptions, and slower-than-expected adoption of new deposition technologies could moderate growth.
Overall, the market is poised for steady expansion, with value migrating toward suppliers offering high-purity, application-specific precursors and integrated service offerings.
Demand Drivers and Constraints
Primary Demand Drivers
- Advanced node semiconductor scaling: Each new technology node (e.g., 3nm, 2nm) increases the number of thin-film deposition steps and demands higher-purity precursors, driving volume and value growth.
- Proliferation of ALD and CVD technologies: Atomic layer deposition and chemical vapor deposition are increasingly adopted for their precision and conformality, expanding the range of applications and chemical consumption.
- Rising demand for advanced memory and logic devices: 3D NAND, DRAM, and high-performance logic chips require multiple thin-film layers, boosting precursor demand.
- Growth in display and photovoltaic markets: OLED, microLED, and thin-film solar technologies rely heavily on thin-film deposition, creating new demand streams.
- Government initiatives to onshore semiconductor manufacturing: Policies like the US CHIPS Act and EU Chips Act are stimulating new fab construction, increasing regional demand for thin-film chemicals.
- Increasing electronic content per vehicle: Automotive electronics, ADAS, and EV power electronics require thin-film components, driving demand for specialty chemicals.
Potential Growth Constraints
- High qualification and validation burdens: Thin-film chemicals for semiconductor applications require lengthy and costly qualification cycles, slowing time-to-market for new entrants.
- Volatility in raw material prices: Precursors often rely on rare metals and specialty chemicals, exposing the market to price fluctuations and supply disruptions.
- Stringent environmental and safety regulations: Compliance with REACH, TSCA, and other regulations increases operational costs and complexity.
- Cyclicality in semiconductor demand: The market is tied to the semiconductor capital expenditure cycle, which can lead to periods of oversupply and price erosion.
- Technical complexity and IP barriers: Developing and manufacturing high-purity precursors requires deep expertise and patented technologies, limiting competition.
Demand Structure by End-Use Industry
End-Use Industry Demand Split (%)
Semiconductor Foundry & IDM (estimated share: 45%)
The semiconductor foundry and integrated device manufacturer (IDM) segment is the largest and most critical end-use sector for thin-film chemicals, accounting for approximately 45% of global demand. This segment's demand is driven by the continuous scaling of logic and memory devices, where each new technology node introduces additional thin-film deposition steps and more complex precursor chemistries. For instance, the transition from 7nm to 5nm and 3nm nodes significantly increases the use of atomic layer deposition (ALD) for gate dielectrics, spacers, and barrier layers, requiring high-purity precursors such as hafnium, zirconium, and titanium compounds.
The demand is also supported by capacity expansions in leading-edge fabs in Taiwan, South Korea, and the United States. Key demand-side indicators include wafer starts, capital expenditure by foundries and IDMs, and the ramp of new nodes. Through 2035, the segment is expected to grow at a CAGR of 7.2%, driven by the adoption of gate-all-around (GAA) transistors, 3D NAND with more than 200 layers, and advanced packaging technologies like chiplets and 3D stacking. The qualification burden is extremely high, with suppliers needing to meet stringent purity and reliability standards. Major companies in this segment include TSMC, Samsung, Intel, GlobalFoundries, and SK Hynix, which are both consumers and drivers of thin-film chemical demand.
Current trend: Growing.
Major trends: Transition to gate-all-around (GAA) transistors at 3nm and below, Increasing layer count in 3D NAND (200+ layers), Adoption of advanced packaging (chiplets, 3D stacking), Growth in EUV lithography enabling new deposition steps, and Regionalization of semiconductor supply chains.
Representative participants: TSMC, Samsung Electronics, Intel Corporation, GlobalFoundries, SK Hynix, and Micron Technology.
Display & Optoelectronics (estimated share: 20%)
The display and optoelectronics segment represents approximately 20% of the thin-film chemicals market, driven by the production of OLED, microLED, and advanced LCD displays, as well as optical coatings for sensors and photonics. Thin-film chemicals are used in the deposition of transparent conductive oxides (e.g., ITO), barrier layers, and emissive layers. The demand is fueled by the rising adoption of OLED displays in smartphones, TVs, and wearables, and the emergence of microLED technology for high-end displays. Additionally, the growth of augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) devices requires high-performance optical coatings, boosting demand for specialty precursors.

Lam Research, the world's No. 1 etch equipment maker, is further expanding its collaboration with South Korea's semiconductor ecosystem. Following the shipment of its 15,000th semiconductor manufacturing chamber from its South Korean production facilities, the U.S. company is now establishing a dedicated venture investment fund targeting South Korean startups.
Lam Research announced these plans on the 8th at the inaugural "Lam Research Supplier Symposium Korea" held in Gyeonggi Province. Tim Archer, chairman and CEO of Lam Research, said at the event: "In the AI era, with rising demand and increasing technological complexity, the speed of problem-solving and the ability to ramp new technologies into high-volume manufacturing are more critical than ever. Through closer collaboration, we will deliver the speed our customers require and the innovation the industry needs."
The chamber that reached the 15,000-unit shipment milestone is a core component inside the equipment where wafers are loaded and actual processes such as etching and deposition take place. Lam Research has been producing semiconductor equipment in South Korea for the past 15 years, centered on three production facilities in Gyeonggi Province—Osan, Hwaseong, and Yongin. The company also operates the Korea Technology Center (KTC), an R&D hub, in Yongin.
The company emphasized that the 15,000th chamber shipment demonstrates its standing as the largest front-end semiconductor equipment manufacturer in South Korea and the largest wafer fabrication equipment exporter in the country. It marks another milestone following last year's procurement of products and services from South Korean partners exceeding 1 trillion won (approximately $744.6 million).
Supply Chain Collaboration Expanding Beyond the Capital Region
Lam Research currently maintains a supply chain network with approximately 100 South Korean companies, a significant portion of which are small and medium-sized enterprises. The company said its South Korean partners have strengthened their technical capabilities and expanded business opportunities into overseas markets through joint engineering projects, quality management programs, and participation in the global supply chain.
The geographic scope of supply chain collaboration is also expanding. Lam Research explained that it is increasing cooperation with companies across various regions of South Korea, moving beyond the existing semiconductor industry cluster concentrated in the capital region.
In August, Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, Semes, Lam Research Korea, and Wonik IPS jointly participated in a seminar on ceramic materials and components for semiconductor processes in Gumi, North Gyeongsang Province. The event covered ceramic materials used in etch and deposition equipment chambers, as well as particle reduction technologies.
First Country-Level Strategic Investment Program
At the event, Lam Research announced that Lam Capital, its corporate venture investment arm, and Hana Ventures will jointly establish the "Lam Research-Hana Semiconductor Unicorn Fund." This marks the first time Lam Research has created a country-level strategic semiconductor investment program.
The fund's primary investment targets are South Korean startups with next-generation semiconductor technologies in manufacturing AI, robotics, advanced packaging, and new materials. The plan extends beyond simple capital investment to include technology validation, commercialization, and support for global market entry. The vision is to connect Lam Research's equipment and process technologies with the innovative technologies of South Korean startups.
Lam Research recently built the "Velocity Lab" at its Yongin R&D hub, where new materials can be rapidly validated and innovative ideas can be co-developed with customers, partners, and collaborators. It is expected to serve as infrastructure for collaboration with startups.
Lam Research opened its first office in South Korea in 1989 and has steadily expanded its business foundation through production, R&D, supply chain collaboration, and talent development. The company said that as of 2025, its South Korean operations have generated more than 13 trillion won (approximately $9.7 billion) in economic impact and contributed to the creation of more than 25,000 direct and indirect jobs.
Semiconductor manufacturing involves repeated cycles of lithography to etch fine circuits onto wafers, deposition to apply thin films, etching to remove unnecessary material, and cleaning processes. Etch equipment, where Lam Research holds the world's top competitive position, is used to precisely carve circuit patterns on wafers or create microscopic holes. Major South Korean semiconductor companies, including Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, are key customers of Lam Research equipment.

A little less than seven months since signing a memorandum of understanding (MOU) concerning memory supply and collaboration in various fields with Samsung, AMD's chief executive Lisa Su is visiting South Korea to secure additional supply of HBM memory for AI accelerators, reports Chosun.biz. Meanwhile, Samsung is seeking a broader partnership and 'hopes to turn its memory supply relationship with AMD into foundry' chip production orders, the report claims.
"We are going to talk about our broader partnership," said Lisa Su when asked by reporters about what she planned to discuss with Samsung's executives. "We have many partners at Samsung."
Before visiting Samsung headquarters, Lisa Su and Jack Huynh, senior vice president and general manager of AMD's Computing and Graphics Group, attended the AMD Gamer Day event where Su and Huynh answered some questions from South Korean journalists and called local memory makers 'important strategic partners,' something that reflects the significance of data center-grade DDR5 and HBM memory for the company's AI and data center businesses.
"Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are key supply-chain partners for AMD," Su said, Chosun reports. "AI demand is extremely high, so we are planning our long-term supply chain with our partners. […] It is important to plan three to five years ahead with our partners."
The non-binding MOU that AMD and Samsung signed this March covered four areas and remained in effect for a period of three years:
- Supply of next-generation memory products, including HBM4 and advanced DDR5;
- Co-development and optimization of memory solutions for Al and high-performance computing systems;
- Exploration of foundry manufacturing opportunities for the future AMD platforms;
- Co-optimization of advanced packaging and related semiconductor technologies.
While Samsung has become a principal supplier of HBM4 for AMD's Instinct MI400-series accelerators, expansion of collaboration beyond memory supply is considerably more complicated, as it involves considerable efforts to design chips for Samsung Foundry's process technologies as well as risks associated with a product ramp at a new contract chipmaker. Truth to be told, AMD already uses Samsung Foundry and UMC to make its "ICs in the form of programmable logic devices" however, moving production of more advanced products to Samsung is risky. Meanwhile, Samsung badly needs big customers like AMD, and the latter's dependence on HBM supply certainly gives the former leverage.
"If we transition the production of some of our products to new manufacturers, we may experience delayed product introductions, lower yields or poorer performance of our products," AMD wrote in its most recent Annual Report.

AMD has already started shipments of its Instinct MI455 accelerators with 432GB of HBM4 memory onboard as well as rack-scale Helios AI systems to interested parties.
"We have started shipping our next-generation MI455 and Helios systems," Su told journalists, according to Chosun. "These are all systems that use HBM4."
So, it looks like the company is negotiating for more memory supply. The question is, will it take a risk and adopt Samsung Foundry for something more serious than niche programmable chips in a bid to get more high-bandwidth memory and sell more expensive AI accelerators? Only time will tell.

FSR 4 started as a Radeon 9000 exclusive technology when it was unveiled at CES 2025, but community efforts to port the AMD machine learning upscaler to older architectures - including that of the Steam Machine - quickly proved that a wider rollout was possible. The tech hit Radeon 7000 graphics cards in July, with Radeon 6000 models set to get official support by next year. Now, it looks like another square on the bingo card is being filled in, as FSR 4 is officially arriving for the AMD APUs that power gaming handhelds, laptops and mini PCs.
The news comes from AMD senior vice president and general manager of the computing and graphics group, Jack Huynh, who spoke to media in Korea including TheElec.
"We will expand the machine learning AI-based FSR 4 technology, which was first introduced to existing discrete graphics cards, to the entire product line - including APUs, gaming laptops and handheld devices by the end of the year", he said. As well as coming to existing models, Huynh also stated that FSR 4 would be a part of "new product lines."
The new product line would presumably be based on an RDNA 4 graphics component with hardware acceleration for ML-based upscaling, frame generation, ray reconstruction and other FSR 4 components, while existing products will get a lightweight FSR 4 model that is more performant on APUs without hardware acceleration that therefore struggle with the full-fat model. "We have newly developed a dedicated lightweight model that suits the APU environment... we are focusing on excellent game image quality and low latency", Huynh stated.
As we saw with the recently announced QSSR from Sony, such an approach can be extremely effective, establishing a middle tier that offers better image quality and stability than older analytical upscalers like FSR 3, while running faster than full-fat FSR 4.
In an age where new hardware is becoming increasingly unaffordable, stretching existing silicon to support more effective upscaling techniques is one of the few ways to keep graphical fidelity and performance moving forward. These early community FSR 4 ports have already proven useful, so it will be interesting to see how the official AMD implementation surpasses them - if at all.

Special Coverage
“Range matters now”: Microsoft’s Puneet Chandok, GrowthSchool’s Vaibhav Sisinty on the skills that will define Gen Z careers
India will release a consultation paper on artificial intelligence (AI) regulation within a month, Union Minister for Electronics and Information Technology Ashwini Vaishnaw said on Thursday, October 8, signalling the Centre's next step towards developing a regulatory framework that addresses deepfakes, cybersecurity risks, psychological harm and user safety.
Speaking at an event centred on a World Bank report on AI, Vaishnaw said the proposed consultation paper would form the foundation for future regulation, with industry expected to take significant responsibility for addressing risks associated with the technology.
"Secretary Krishnan spoke about AI regulation, yes, time has come. I request the department to come out with a regulation focused consultation paper which focusses on safety, that is the most important point, safety related to AI use," Vaishnaw said.
The minister outlined five broad priorities for the proposed framework: safety, a human-first approach, skilling, inclusion and addressing societal harms caused by AI.
Industry to shoulder responsibility for AI-related harms
Vaishnaw stressed that regulating AI would require more than conventional legislation, calling for a combination of technological safeguards, legal measures and industry participation.
"We have always maintained that AI and technologies cannot be regulated just by having a law. We have to bring a techno-legal solution," he said.
The minister indicated that technology companies would be expected to assume considerable responsibility for managing risks associated with their systems, particularly cybersecurity, user safety, deepfakes and psychological harm.
"Bulk of the responsibility will have to be taken by the industry, especially on cyber security, on safety, on user harm, on psychological disorders that might come and on deepfakes," he said.
His remarks place industry accountability at the centre of the government's proposed approach, even as the precise regulatory obligations and enforcement mechanisms remain to be outlined.
Deepfakes and psychological risks emerge as key concerns
Among the risks highlighted by Vaishnaw, deepfakes received particular attention, with the minister warning that increasingly sophisticated AI-generated content could mislead users and create wider societal consequences.
He described deepfakes as a form of harmful output that could cause significant problems as their quality and believability continue to improve.
"People believe them and the quality of deepfakes is increasing every day," he said, warning that such content could create misleading narratives and influence people into taking harmful decisions.
Vaishnaw also called for psychological risks associated with AI use to be explicitly addressed in the consultation paper.
"Many of these harms are also related to psychological disorders which come because of the way AI can lure people. So please include that also in your consultation paper," he said.
The proposed framework will also examine how AI adoption can remain inclusive, particularly as the technology creates uneven economic and social benefits.
The minister acknowledged that while some sections of society stand to benefit substantially from AI-led productivity and economic gains, others could feel excluded from the transition.
Government estimates demand for 10,000 GPUs, first tender for 5,000
Alongside the proposed regulatory framework, Vaishnaw outlined the government's plans to strengthen AI infrastructure and public-sector adoption.
He said the Centre estimates demand for 10,000 graphics processing units (GPUs), with the first tender covering 5,000 GPUs.
"Our demand estimate is for 10,000 GPUs and the first tender that we are coming out is for 5,000," he said.
The government is also pursuing five-year supply agreements intended to provide companies with greater demand visibility and encourage longer-term investments in AI infrastructure.
Vaishnaw said the department had issued a request for empanelment the previous day as part of the procurement initiative.
For AI adoption across government departments, the Centre plans to establish an empanelment mechanism through which eligible AI models, solutions and startups can qualify to participate in departmental tenders.
"It won't be a tender process. It will be an empanelment process," he said, explaining that selected companies would subsequently be able to bid for government projects requiring AI technologies.
India targets indigenous GPUs for AI inference in three to four years
Vaishnaw also indicated that India is working towards developing domestic GPU capabilities, particularly for AI inference, over the next three to four years.
He said a clearer technological roadmap had recently emerged under the country's semiconductor efforts, making it possible to pursue an Indian alternative for certain AI computing requirements.
According to the minister, the roadmap had not been discussed publicly earlier because the path towards developing such capabilities was not sufficiently clear.
"But now that roadmap is visible and we can say that in three to four years time frame, India, our talent pool which has the capabilities will be able to come up with a solution which can become a good solution for the country and for the global sector," he said.
The minister added that further progress on the initiative would be shared in the coming weeks and months.
AI curriculum overhaul and adoption across agriculture, healthcare
On the talent development front, Vaishnaw said the government has worked with industry to prepare an updated curriculum for AI-related education, which has been shared with the Ministry of Education.
Joint workshops involving the ministry and industry are expected to help universities and colleges adopt the revised curriculum.
The minister also highlighted examples of AI applications delivering measurable gains in agriculture, healthcare and dairy production.
In Baramati, he said, the combination of satellite information, IoT sensors, weather intelligence and farm-level data had helped increase sugarcane yields by 40%, while reducing labour costs by 20–40% and water and fertiliser use by 30%.
Similarly, he said AI-enabled agricultural services in Gujarat were being used by more than five lakh farmers, while an AI application serving the dairy ecosystem was benefiting 26 lakh milk producers and covering three crore cattle.
Vaishnaw argued that AI's economic value would increasingly come from practical applications that help individuals and smaller businesses access capabilities previously available mainly to larger enterprises.
He also pointed to the potential of smaller, fine-tuned open-weight AI models to deliver better results than frontier models on narrowly defined tasks.
While describing India's AI journey as promising, the minister cautioned that scaling the technology would involve social, technical and regulatory challenges.
The government's forthcoming consultation paper, he indicated, would seek to balance the benefits of broader AI adoption with safeguards addressing risks to individuals and society.

Applause erupted at the Nuri Launch Control Center (LCC) as the fifth Nuri rocket, launched at 12:25 p.m. on October 7 from the Naro Space Center in Goheung, Jeonnam-Gwangju, successfully deployed four miniature cluster satellites, NeonSats, into the target orbit. The launch control center, which oversees the entire Nuri launch process, had 23 Hanwha Aerospace employees involved this time. The Korea Aerospace Research Institute (KARI) stepped back to a supervisory role. Following the selection of Hanwha Aerospace as the system integrator for the fourth Nuri launch, the launch operation has now been fully transferred to the private sector.
Industry sources said, “This is a symbolic scene showing the dawn of a private-sector-led space industry era.” Over 300 domestic companies participated in the production and launch of the fifth Nuri rocket, with defense companies playing a particularly significant role. Hanwha Aerospace supplied key components, including the 75-ton liquid rocket engine, and oversaw the overall assembly of the launch vehicle. Hyundai Rotem provided propulsion system test facilities, while Korea Aerospace Industries (KAI) manufactured the first-stage propulsion system. HD Hyundai Heavy Industries designed and built the launchpad systems, including ground mechanical facilities and propulsion supply systems.
◇ Defense Big 4 Transforming into Space Enterprises
Space projects, once led by governments, have shifted toward private-sector dominance with the emergence of SpaceX’s reusable Falcon 9 rockets and Starlink satellite communications. While Chinese and Japanese private companies like LandSpace and Honda have succeeded in developing and testing reusable launch vehicles, South Korea’s defense companies—having accumulated capabilities in military-related aerospace projects such as satellites, rocket launchers, and engines—are now leading market expansion.
Hyundai Rotem reorganized its defense business division into the AD (Aerospace·Defense) & RH (Robot & Hydrogen) division in the second half of the year, elevating its space business to the forefront. The new organization focuses on engines for reusable launch vehicles. Since the 2000s, Hyundai Rotem has researched and developed methane engines for launch vehicles. Methane is highly praised for its superior thrust and minimal soot, making it ideal for reusable launch vehicles. Hyundai Rotem plans to invest 300 billion Korean won to establish a methane engine research, development, and production base in Muju County, North Jeolla Province.
Hanwha Aerospace aims to become a comprehensive system integrator for reusable launch vehicles. On October 30, it began assembling a test reusable rocket with KARI, with plans to complete flight tests for launch and landing by 2028. The company intends to enter the space transportation service market by creating a Korean version of the Falcon 9. Hanwha Aerospace is also developing a propulsion system for a lunar lander scheduled for launch in 2032 with KARI.
◇ KAI·LIG Expanding Satellite Industry… Challenging a Korean Starlink
KAI, which has focused on medium-to-large satellite manufacturing for over 30 years, is expanding into the miniature satellite sector. Just as SpaceX dominates the satellite communication market with its Starlink constellation of miniature satellites, KAI aims to preempt the Korean miniature satellite market. A KAI official said, “We have established a system capable of producing over 100 miniature satellites annually at the Sacheon Space Center in South Gyeongsang Province.”
LIG D&A, which launched its space business division in January last year and declared its entry into the space industry, is also focusing on satellite projects. In April last year, it was selected as the developer for the Cheollian Satellite 5, South Korea’s first privately led geostationary satellite. In October of the same year, it completed the assembly facility for satellites and laser systems in Daejeon with an investment of 100 billion Korean won.

The current market volume, while growing, remains constrained by the historical adoption curves of LFP batteries, which saw significant uptake first in China for buses and fleet vehicles, followed by global expansion in passenger EVs and energy storage systems (ESS) over the last decade. The electric vehicle segment is the primary source of spent LFP battery feedstock, driven by the massive adoption of LFP chemistry in EVs, especially in China and Europe. Currently, most feedstock comes from manufacturing scrap and early recalls, but the volume of end-of-life batteries will surge after 2028 as vehicles sold in the early 2010s retire. Demand-side indicators include EV sales penetration rates, average battery lifespan, and government recycling mandates. By 2035, this segment will dominate, with collection networks maturing and OEMs taking responsibility for take-back schemes.
The shift towards circularity will be accelerated by regulations requiring minimum recycled content in new batteries, creating a closed-loop demand for recovered materials. Current trend: Rapidly increasing as first-generation EVs reach end-of-life.
Major trends: OEM-led battery take-back programs, Integration of recycling into EV manufacturing, Government mandates for recycling efficiency, and Growth of LFP in commercial fleets.
Representative participants: Tesla, BYD, CATL, Volkswagen, and GM.
Energy storage systems (ESS) using LFP chemistry are a rapidly growing source of spent feedstock, driven by the global transition to renewable energy. Grid-scale and residential ESS installations have surged, particularly in China, the US, and Europe. These systems typically have a lifespan of 10-15 years, meaning the first wave of spent ESS batteries will enter the recycling stream in the late 2020s. Demand-side indicators include renewable energy capacity additions, government auctions for storage, and corporate sustainability targets. By 2035, ESS will contribute a significant share, with second-life applications potentially delaying recycling but ultimately feeding into the loop.
The segment's growth is supported by declining LFP costs and safety advantages. Current trend: Growing steadily with increasing deployments of grid-scale storage.
Major trends: Second-life applications for ESS, Modular design for easier disassembly, Policy support for storage deployment, and Corporate PPAs driving storage.
Representative participants: Sungrow, Fluence, Tesla, BYD, and LG Energy Solution.
Consumer electronics represent a smaller but consistent source of spent LFP batteries, primarily from power tools, e-bikes, and portable power stations. LFP is less common in smartphones and laptops due to lower energy density, but its use in high-drain devices is growing. The feedstock volume is constrained by long product lifespans and low collection rates. However, increasing awareness and right-to-repair legislation are expected to improve collection. Demand-side indicators include sales of cordless power tools and e-bikes, and recycling rates. By 2035, this segment will remain a minor contributor but will benefit from standardized collection systems and modular battery designs.
Current trend: Stable but limited due to smaller battery sizes and longer replacement cycles.
Major trends: Right-to-repair legislation, Growth in e-bike and power tool sales, Modular battery design, and Retailer take-back programs.
Representative participants: Stanley Black & Decker, Bosch, Makita, Xiaomi, and Anker.
Industrial backup power applications, including telecom towers, data centers, and uninterruptible power supplies (UPS), are increasingly adopting LFP batteries due to their longer cycle life and safety. The feedstock from this segment is generated when these batteries are replaced after 8-12 years of service. Demand-side indicators include telecom infrastructure expansion, data center growth, and replacement cycles. By 2035, this segment will provide a steady stream of spent batteries, with collection often managed by service providers. The shift from lead-acid to LFP is expected to accelerate, driven by total cost of ownership and environmental regulations.
Current trend: Increasing as LFP replaces lead-acid in telecom and UPS applications.
Major trends: Replacement of lead-acid with LFP, Growth in data center UPS, Telecom tower upgrades, and Service-based battery management.
Representative participants: Eaton, Vertiv, Schneider Electric, Huawei, and ZTE.
Marine and recreational vehicle (RV) applications are a niche but growing source of spent LFP batteries, as LFP is favored for its deep-cycle capability and safety. The feedstock volume is small due to the limited number of units and long replacement cycles (often 10+ years). However, the increasing popularity of electric boats and RVs is expected to boost future volumes. Demand-side indicators include boat and RV sales, and the adoption rate of LFP over lead-acid. By 2035, this segment will remain minor but will benefit from improved collection networks and recycling awareness among enthusiasts. Current trend: Niche but growing as LFP becomes preferred for deep-cycle applications.
Major trends: Electrification of marine vessels, Growth in RV market, LFP as drop-in replacement for lead-acid, and Marina and dealership take-back.
