The United Arab Emirates (UAE) is on course to become the fourth space power to touch an asteroid, according to scientists and engineers involved in the country’s space programme. On 1 October, they announced the completion of a probe that is expected to career into the reddish rock known as Justicia in 2035.
The probe was designed and built in the UAE. It will now be shipped to the University of Colorado Boulder, where collaborators will integrate it with the main MBR Explorer spacecraft before a launch scheduled for March 2028.
The Emirates Mission to the Asteroid belt (EMA) will observe six asteroids using an array of cameras and spectrometers, which can analyse material composition remotely. It will also observe Venus and Mars, before the MBR Explorer spacecraft dispatches the tiny 10 kilogram probe to its final destination, the asteroid Justicia.
Justicia’s unusual red colour suggests that the asteroid contains materials more commonly found further out in the Solar System than its current orbit between Mars and Jupiter. If it originated in the outer reaches and migrated inwards, that makes it an ancient “traveller from the past” that could give clues as to how the Solar System formed and the origins of its water, said Elias Tsoutsanis, chief researcher for the Propulsion and Space Research Center at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi. The TII is a government-backed research agency that designed and developed the probe. Tsoutsanis was speaking at an event in the city on 1 October marking the probe’s completion.
The UAE’s relatively quick ascent into the club of space-faring nations has come through a programme of hiring international partners who have helped to design and build their various spacecraft while also training Emirati researchers and engineers.
The progress on the latest mission shows the UAE’s growing independence in space science and technology, said computer scientist Najwa Aaraj, chief executive of the TII, at the 1 October event. Whereas every part of Hope was a collaboration, the UAE built the probe component of the EMA on its own. “I’m very confident that in the next mission, we don’t need Colorado,” she added. “Everything can be done end-to-end here.”
The country’s activities in the skies seem to be having an impact on the ground. Since the UAE announced its plan to send a mission to Mars in 2014, there has been a 30% rise in students enrolling in science, technology, engineering and mathematics, said Ahmad Belhoul Al Falasi, chair of the UAE Space Agency, at the event. Between 2015 and 2025, the number of UAE universities offering aerospace engineering and space-related degree programmes has roughly doubled, he later told Nature.

articles.title: Daily briefing: Chemistry Nobel goes to mirror-molecule researchers
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03212-xHenri Kagan and Kenso Soai have won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Plus, the biggest success stories in cancer survival and one of the biggest debates in neuroscience.

Chemistry Nobel for ‘handed’ molecules
Chemists Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have won this year’s Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their work on a long-standing mystery: how can living organisms create molecules that are just one of two possible mirror-image variants? In the 1980s, Kagan showed how catalysts can amplify a small asymmetry in handedness. And in the 1990s, Soai demonstrated that a one-handed molecule, produced in a reaction, can become its own catalyst, driving even greater asymmetry. Together they provided clues as to how natural reactions in living organisms might overwhelmingly produce just one type of mirror-image molecule.
News
The top cancer success stories
Seventy-one percent of people with cancer in the United States live for at least five years after diagnosis, up from 49% in the late 1970s, says a new report. Highlights include huge strides against lung cancer and childhood leukaemias. In some cases, the numbers tell a nuanced story: the five-year survival rate for prostate cancer is now nearly 98% — a figure so high that it suggests some of the tumours were not malignant to start with, says cancer epidemiologist Rebecca Siegel.
Reference: American Association for Cancer Research report
Sharks have surprisingly sharp hearing
Blacktip sharks (Carcharhinus limbatus) can hear and respond to sounds up to 74 metres away — beyond the radius that scientists thought the animals’ hearing was restricted to. Researchers found that the sharks often turned sharply away from speakers playing certain frequencies of noise, which suggests they could tell where it was coming from. A response at this distance “suggests that they are detecting the particle motion associated with sound”, which hasn’t been observed in sharks before, says zoologist and study co-author Stephen Kajiura.
Reference: Integrative Organismal Biology paper
Image of the week
In hospital isolation wards, health workers who treat people with Ebola must don time-consuming and uncomfortable protective suits. Intensive-care physician Richard Kojan and his colleagues developed the CUBE (emergency biosecurity chamber for epidemics), which allows them to treat highly contagious people in the field without the stifling suits. The 9-metre-square room can be set up in 90 minutes. “When we introduced the CUBE, we invited patients’ relatives into the facilities to see their family members through the plastic walls of the unit,” says Kojan. “It had never been possible to see and spend time with their loved ones before. This has had a huge social impact and helped to resolve tensions.” (Nature | 9 min read)
Read more in Nature Spotlight: Infectious diseases. (Elie BIGABA / ALIMA)
Features & opinion
The great neurogenesis debate
A growing body of evidence hints that the human brain can produce new nerve cells throughout a person’s life, challenging the long-held belief that people are born with all the neurons they’ll ever have. If that’s true, our brains could have an enduring ability to repair and regenerate. But neuroscientists remain divided, and influential papers have come down on both sides of the argument. Still, some think that the evidence is strong enough to shift focus onto potential applications of neurogenesis, such as treating neurodegenerative disease.
‘They made the science their own’
Earlier this year, a team of nanoscientists visited a local primary school to give a lesson on their work. To give the kids a sense of just how small ‘nano’ is, a teacher wrote 0.000000001 on a whiteboard. The children quickly adorned the number with a face, antennae and legs — the ‘nanopillar’ was born. The student “made the science their own”, the team writes. The group uses these visits both to inspire young children and to test themselves: “if we cannot explain our research to a second grader, then we probably do not understand it as well as we think we do”, they say.

articles.title: OpenAI posts 700 maths preprints online: mathematicians are up in arms
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03196-8The firm used unreleased models to tackle hundreds of high-profile problems.

The research community is in uproar after OpenAI released a trove of more than 700 mathematical preprints entirely generated by AI on 6 October. The San Francisco, California-based maker of ChatGPT posted the preprints on the software repository Github.
Although some mathematicians celebrated the solution of longstanding problems, others took to social media to complain about being scooped. Some were incensed at what one physicist called a ‘slopocalypse’, even if the mathematical content could end up being formally correct.
The sheer number of papers posted at the same time is “staggering”, wrote Alvaro Lozano-Robledo, a number theorist at the University of Connecticut in Storrs, on the social-media platform X. “Why is OpenAI trying to solve hundreds of math problems to be released all at once?”, he added.
In an e-mail to Nature, a spokesperson for OpenAI wrote that the company’s goal is to provide tools for mathematicians and scientists. “To accomplish this, we evaluate and develop our models against difficult frontier problems in all sciences.”
Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at rival company Anthropic, also in San Francisco, commented on X that there will be “sad stories” for some researchers who might find their projects pre-empted by the OpenAI release. “We should put that aside for today though. It’s obviously the most significant moment in mathematical history,” he wrote, because it shows how quickly the technology has become useful to mathematicians.
Prized problems
The large batch of preprints did not include any solutions to the five remaining ‘Millennium Prize Problems’, selected by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which has its scientific headquarters in Oxford, UK, at the turn of the twenty-first century. (OpenAI’s preprint on the Navier-Stokes equation, released in September, solved one of the original seven problems. Another one was solved by mathematicians in the early 2000s.)
Still, some of the preprints were on problems related to those five, including the Hodge conjecture on complex algebraic varieties and the Riemann hypothesis on the statistical properties of prime numbers. The spokesperson for OpenAI said, “We will leave it to the broader community to assess [their] significance.”
